standards: Explain why a bank reconciliation is done every month and describe what a finished, fully explained reconciliation looks like, naming how it helps catch errors and fraud early.
Read a bank list and a ledger list side by side and identify each line, so that every entry on both lists is correctly understood before matching begins.
Match the lines of a bank list to a ledger list and classify each difference as a timing item, such as an uncleared cheque or a deposit not yet recorded.
Complete the reconciliation statement in the set layout, adjusting both balances with timing and ledger items until the difference after reconciling is zero.
Spot unusual items such as unexplained small amounts, round sums or duplicates, then explain each one, record it against the set limit and escalate when required.
Reconcile a full practice file of twelve bank lines and twelve ledger lines, finding all three planted differences and finishing with a correct signed statement.
Complete a timed assessment reconciliation by matching items, writing the statement and explaining every difference, meeting the checklist with no unexplained balance left.
Explain what a board expects on a single page, choosing a few figures that each carry a one-line meaning rather than listing every number.
Calculate the six ratios, current, quick, gross margin, net margin, debtor days and creditor days, from a set of statements using the correct formulas.
Compare each ratio with last year's figure and state the direction and pace of change, because a single number means little without a reference.
Explain a change in a ratio in plain words, giving a likely cause and a suggested action, as in the liquidity worked example.
Build a one-page summary from two years of statements, showing six ratios, a plain-words note on each change and the source of the numbers.
Complete a timed assessment by computing the ratios from invented statements and writing a one-page summary that meets every checklist point.
Find the official source of a rule change, check its date and confirm what it says, and state plainly when you are unsure and must refer on.
Write a summary of a rule change in about one hundred words that states what changes, from when, and what the client should do.
Work out the effect of a rule change on a sample client using last year's figures, and show it as a short worked example in the client's terms.
Cite the official source and its date in every client note, and file the note with the source in the client file.
Practise writing a client note from a short invented rule change, then use the feedback to correct gaps in source, date and example.
Check your finished note against the list: source cited, date stated, worked example included, and any doubt referred to a senior.
Define a conflict of interest in plain words and recognise it in everyday examples where personal or firm gain could affect your duty to the client.
Judge eight short cases, marking each as a conflict or not a conflict and naming the action that fits, such as declaring, avoiding or asking.
Use the firm's approved disclosure wording to tell a client about a conflict before giving any advice, in writing.
Record each conflict, the action taken and the named approver in the register, so the decision can be traced later.
Practise deciding, disclosing and recording on a new case, such as a fund run by a relative, and correct any step you missed.
Show in a short check that you can define a conflict, take the first step of declaring it and record it with the approver.
Explain why an advice review exists and why a written record of the match between client and product must show the thought behind the advice.
Collect the essential facts from a client card, goals, time horizon, comfort with loss and financial position, and refuse to proceed while facts are missing.
Match a client's needs to a suitable product type, considering alternatives, using the facts gathered and the client's own words on risk comfort.
Write the reason for the match in plain words so that another person can see why the product fitted the client.
Complete the advice record to the checklist, including alternatives considered, client confirmation, and the signatures required of the adviser and client.
Complete a practice file for an invented client, recording facts, matching a product type and writing the reason, then correct gaps after feedback.
Complete a timed assessment record for a new client card that meets every checklist item and shows a clear written reason for the match.
Recognise warning signs of suspicious activity, such as cash just under a reporting limit, unexplained wealth or reluctance to give identity details.
Review six sample transactions, marking each as concern or no concern and giving a reason for each decision.
Use the local route card to name who receives a report and how quickly it must be made, and send a report by that route.
Explain why the customer must not be told about a report and avoid any words or actions that would warn them.
Practise writing a four-line report covering who, what, when and why it worries you, using facts only, with date and time.
Show in a short check that you know the reporting route, the ban on telling the customer and the content of a report.
Explain why change often fails, including people not knowing the reason, and show why the reason should be given first.
Map the groups affected by a change, such as staff, customers and suppliers, and say how each group is touched.
Plan three messages for a change, each with a set time and a named sender, so the most affected group hears first from their own manager.
Respond to worry and resistance by listening, finding the cause and adjusting the support offered, rather than repeating the message.
Choose three simple measures for a change, such as errors per 100 items or briefing attendance, and say how each will be read.
Apply the whole method to a case such as moving from paper forms to an online form, mapping groups, planning messages and picking measures.
Complete a timed assessment on a new change case by mapping groups, writing a first message and choosing measures that meet the checklist.
Set a target, a limit and a walk-away point before a negotiation, writing each number down and stating that the limit is the worst deal you will accept.
Choose three trades you can offer, such as a longer term for a lower price, and say what each trade is worth to you.
Ask open questions and listen closely to find what the other side really needs, so that trades can be matched to those needs.
Carry out a role-play negotiation against a supplier asking for a higher price, staying inside your limit and using at least one trade.
Carry out a second role-play that includes a twist, such as a new demand, and adjust your trades while keeping to your limit.
Write a one-page summary of the agreed price, term, delivery, payment, review date and signatory, ready for sign-off by the person with authority.
Complete a timed assessment by preparing numbers, negotiating a role-play and producing a summary that meets every checklist point.
Describe the one-page shape of a business case, listing the parts it must contain and keeping it to a single page.
State a problem in two lines and set out the options, including a do-nothing option as the baseline for comparison.
List costs and benefits for each option and cite where each number came from, marking any guess as an estimate.
Make a clear recommendation with the reason for it, and state the main risk with a plan to reduce it, plus a dated next step.
Write a practice page on a case such as a second delivery van, then use the feedback to correct any missing part.
Check a finished page against the list of parts, sources, risk and length, then correct any gap before it is passed on.
